subs.l000: !What's the perfect revenge on someone who betrayed you?
subs.l001: Two thousand years ago, a man was handed a box.
subs.l002: Inside were the names of everyone who betrayed him.
subs.l003: All he had to do was open it.
subs.l004: Instead, he threw it into the fire.
subs.l007: Ten years earlier, one general's name was spreading along Rome's eastern frontier.
subs.l008: In the war with Parthia, he drove all the way to the enemy's capital.
subs.n1: Born in Syria, he was a general known for discipline harsh enough to frighten his own men.
subs.l011: The emperor trusted him. He gave him the entire East.
subs.l012: The armies, the provinces, even the power to wage war.
subs.l013: Spring, 175 AD. The emperor was far away, on the Danube frontier.
subs.l014: At fifty-four, he had spent winter after winter in a tent.
subs.l015: And that year, the emperor collapsed.
subs.l016: The illness was serious, and the rumors moved faster than he could.
subs.l017: His heir, his son Commodus, was only thirteen.
subs.l018: At his side, the empress Faustina was afraid.
subs.l019: If her husband died, what would happen to their boy?
subs.l020: One account says she wrote to Cassius in secret.
subs.l021: If the emperor dies, she asked, take the empire.
subs.l022: Remember that letter. No one knows the truth.
subs.l025: In April 175, Cassius stood before his army and declared himself emperor.
subs.l026: “The emperor is dead. Rome follows me now.”
subs.l027: Syria and Egypt went over to him.
subs.n2: When Egypt, Rome's breadbasket, fell to him, the Senate declared Cassius a public enemy.
subs.l028: But a few days later, different news arrived.
subs.l030: He could have turned back. He could have called it a mistake.
subs.l032: Only then did the news reach the emperor on the Danube.
subs.l033: It was brought by Martius Verus, governor of Cappadocia.
subs.l034: In that letter was the name of the man he trusted most.
subs.l035: “Him? Why... why him, of all people?”
subs.l036: At first, the emperor kept the news to himself.
subs.n3: Half the empire could become his enemy overnight.
subs.l037: But the rumor spread from tent to tent.
subs.l039: He gathered his men. Everyone expected a speech full of rage.
subs.l040: “Soldiers. I have not come here to rage.”
subs.l041: “I have come to grieve my fate.”
subs.l042: “The friend I held dearest has plotted against me.”
subs.l043: “From this war, I want only one thing.”
subs.l044: “To forgive the man who wronged me.”
subs.l045: “To remain a friend to the one who broke our friendship.”
subs.l047: By every record, he never cursed him.
subs.l048: The only word he used for him was 'ungrateful.'
subs.l049: In the Meditations, there is this line.
subs.l050: “Above all, when you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself.”
subs.l051: Trusting him had been his own choice.
subs.l052: The emperor rushed to end the war in the north.
subs.l053: Barbarian chiefs offered to send troops to help him.
subs.l054: “What happens between Romans is not for your eyes.”
subs.n4: He called his thirteen-year-old son to his side and named him heir.
subs.l055: Then he led his army east.
subs.l056: To meet Cassius alive, and to forgive him.
subs.l059: A centurion named Antonius rode up to Cassius.
subs.l060: The blade caught his neck. The wound was not fatal.
subs.l061: The horse carried on, and another officer finished it.
subs.l063: That was how long he was emperor.
subs.l064: His head was on its way to the emperor.
subs.l066: He ordered it buried before it ever reached him.
subs.l067: “I wanted to meet him alive. Now there is no one left to forgive.”
subs.l069: “The best way to avenge yourself is not to become like the one who wronged you.”
subs.l070: Some time later, a chest arrived before the emperor.
subs.l072: “Senators, generals, governors. Everyone who helped him. It's all in here.”
subs.l075: “If I read these... who will I see tomorrow?”
subs.l077: “No. From tomorrow, I would see a traitor in every face.”
subs.l080: “And so I should become like them?”
subs.l082: Another account says Verus burned them for him.
subs.l083: What is certain is this: those names survive nowhere.
subs.n5: Afterward, the emperor toured the East and showed mercy to the cities that had joined the revolt.
subs.l084: The Senate demanded the conspirators be punished.
subs.l085: “Let no senator's blood be shed in my reign.”
subs.l087: Cassius's son was killed. Others were exiled.
subs.l089: Whether he ever suspected her, the records don't say.
subs.l090: But in his list of things he thanked the gods for, he wrote this.
subs.l091: “That I had such a wife, so loving, and so sincere.”
subs.l094: A business partner. A brother. An old friend.
subs.l095: Imagine the messages that show exactly what they said about you
subs.l096: were in your hand tonight. Would you open them?
subs.l097: Open them, and you get the names. But you carry those names for the rest of your life.
subs.l098: Three ways to beat someone who betrayed you.
subs.l099: One. Don't curse them. Those words only dirty your own mouth.
subs.l100: Two. Don't stand and watch their downfall.
subs.l101: Three. Don't open what you don't need to know.
